By Marines, For Marines

ARTICLE 01

Mission & Values

Why MCSWF exists, and the four values every member is measured against.

Innovation

Embrace and drive continuous improvement in software development methodologies and technologies.

Collaboration

Foster a culture of partnership and open communication across all levels and stakeholders.

Excellence

Strive for the highest standards in software development and delivery, ensuring robust, reliable, and user-centric solutions.

Integrity

Maintain the highest ethical standards in all aspects of operations, earning the trust and confidence of all stakeholders.

Mission

Create a world-class, Marine-led, mission-specific software development capability. Enable Marine modernization efforts by developing applications for commanders at the speed of operations to increase the operating force's lethality and the supporting establishment's efficiency and effectiveness.

Vision

An institutionalized Marine-led software development capability, complete with full career paths in a new occupational field, that revolutionizes how the Marine Corps operates in the digital domain.

MCSWF will become the premier upskilling organization for software development within the Marine Corps and, through partnership with other services and industry, a model for the broader DoD. Through a centralized C2 organization at MCSWF HQ, supported by Data Warfare Platoons at the tactical edge, we will deliver trained Marines capable of producing innovative, mission-focused software solutions — incorporating cutting-edge commercial technology, data science, and AI — that enhance command and control, optimize processes, and accelerate operational efficiencies across all warfighting functions.

The modern battlefield exists over thousands of miles and across multiple domains. MCSWF will address these challenges by supplying commanders with fully trained software Marines, fully enabling them to “locate, close with, and destroy” the enemy.

Endstate

The Marine Corps possesses a scalable organic capability enabling autonomous Marine-led teams that scope and engineer Marine Corps–wide software solutions.

Purpose of this handbook

This handbook gives Marines and staff a one-source document that defines the standards of appearance, conduct, and military customs and courtesy. MCSWF standards are an enforcement and enhancement of Marine Corps standards and orders — they will never violate Marine Corps standards or common expectations for conduct, appearance, and military bearing.

Due to the unique nature of our mission, this is a living document. MCSWF leadership reserves the right to change or adjust it as the organization matures.
ARTICLE 02

Welcome letter

From the Director and the Senior Enlisted Advisor.

On behalf of the Marine Corps Software Factory, we extend our sincerest congratulations on your selection to the MCSWF. You are one of only 18 active-duty Marines chosen to demonstrate that this capability should be an organic part of our uniformed force. We are counting on you to help carry out our vision of expanding technological education and advancing the development of our Marines.

Becoming a member of the MCSWF is not just an achievement you should be proud of; it is a commitment to uphold the highest standards. Marines in the Software Factory will be held to a higher standard than average, with expectations that exceed those of many in the Fleet Marine Force. You will gain more exposure to the Marine Air-Ground Task Force than most Marines. Through the training we provide and your extensive FMF exposure, your knowledge and experience will reach levels that few Marines will ever attain.

In our experience in the Marine Corps, we have witnessed the shift from analog systems to software-defined solutions. We believe this initiative represents the future of the IT community, regardless of MOS, and could potentially evolve into a new military occupational specialty altogether.

You, the new generation of Marines, are the driving force behind making this vision a permanent and sustainable capability for the Marine Corps.

Again, welcome to the Marine Corps Software Factory. You will find your time here personally challenging and professionally rewarding.

ARTICLE 03

Code of Conduct

Marines selected to serve at MCSWF are expected to demonstrate professional and mature behavior at all times, on and off duty.

Marines are required to maintain law-abiding conduct in accordance with local, state, and federal laws, as well as the UCMJ, DoD regulations, Marine Corps policies, and MCSWF guidelines.

All Marines are expected to:

  • Uphold the standards of this handbook, which provides guidance for appropriate actions in all situations.
  • Take responsibility for personal conduct, as it contributes to the overall discipline and order of the unit.
  • Communicate respectfully, addressing others appropriately by rank and name. Civilian and contractor personnel are addressed as “Sir” or “Ma'am” unless directed otherwise.
  • Be punctual and prepared for all meetings, in person or virtual. Cameras on during virtual interactions to enhance communication and emotional intelligence, unless circumstances such as bandwidth dictate otherwise.

Government vs. contractor personnel

You will work alongside government civilians and contractors every day. The line between the two is legal, not social — and crossing it creates real liability. These guidelines come from the Defense Acquisition University's Contracting Officer's Representative training.

Civilian / GS

The government obtains its employees by direct hire under competitive appointment or other civil service procedures. Government personnel are hired, fired, supervised, and rewarded by the government.

Contractor / CTR

Contractor personnel are employees of a contractor, subject to their individual contracts with their employer and to their employer's contract with the government — not to your direction.

Inherently governmental functions

A contractor is prohibited from performing specific functions that are inherently governmental FAR 7.503. Only government officials can legally perform these, because they are so intimately related to the public interest:

  • Direction and control of federal employees
  • Determination of budget policy, guidance, and strategy
  • Resource allocation or program management duties
  • Approval of contractual documents or administering contracts
  • Obligating congressionally authorized funding

Working with contractors

ARTICLE 04

Standards of Appearance

Civilian attire is a privilege extended under MCO 1020.34H, and it can be withdrawn.

  • Marines at Innovation Tower may wear civilian clothing, with grooming standards strictly enforced.
  • Marines must also comply with MC PFT/CFT, the Body Composition and Military Appearance Program. Failure to meet height and weight standards or maintain military appearance may result in assignment to the Body Composition Program or Military Appearance Program.
Administrative action

Any violation of uniform or grooming regulations will result in administrative action. The privilege of civilian attire can be revoked, with the potential consequence of requiring daily wear of the seasonal service uniform.

Civilian attire explorer

Three levels of dress are generally accepted across the DoD. Daily attire at MCSWF is Business Casual unless directed otherwise. Regardless of level, clothing must be clean, well-fitted, and in good condition — torn, faded, or excessively worn clothing is prohibited.

Do's and don'ts

Do

  • When direct guidance is not available, use good situational awareness. Dress for the situation.
  • When TAD, pack extras — laundry service may not be available.
  • Remember you are a professional, in civilian attire or uniform.
  • Consider cultural norms when choosing attire.

Don't

  • Mistake civilian attire for “street” attire. It is not a pass to express your individuality.
  • Overdress. Even in civilian attire, you have a job to do.
  • Wear tank tops, crop tops, or low-cut or revealing tops.
  • Wear dresses or skirts above the knee — they must cover the knees at all times, walking, sitting, and standing.
  • Wear hoodies, unless Marine affiliated.
ARTICLE 05

Fitness & Medical Readiness

Being a software factory changes nothing about MC PFT/CFT.

Marines assigned to MCSWF must annually complete the Physical Fitness Test (PFT) or Partial PFT, and the Combat Fitness Test (CFT) or Partial CFT.

If you fail a test

Consequences of a single failure

An adverse fitness report · impact to proficiency marks · promotion restriction until the test is passed · a required Page 11 or 6105 counseling entry.

Consecutive failures

Failing consecutive PFTs/PPFTs or CFTs/PCFTs — outside of multiple attempts within the same semi-annual reporting period — means consideration for administrative separation.

Worked example. Fail a PFT and a CFT in the same year, and you are not immediately considered for separation. Fail either test the following year, and you are subject to separation proceedings. Pass a retest after a failure but fail that same test the next year, and you are still considered for separation.

Retesting

You may take multiple tests to improve your score during the current season. Every official test is entered into MCTIMS — higher, lower, or the same as previous attempts. Any PFT/CFT monitored by a properly assigned FFI/CPTR is official.

Individual medical readiness

Marines are expected to remain healthy and prepared for duty at all times, and maintaining medical readiness is every Marine's own responsibility. The SEA monitors readiness and distributes monthly notifications.

Our Austin location puts most members on TRICARE Remote. Raise any enrollment issue — yours or your dependents' — to the Senior Enlisted Advisor immediately.

ARTICLE 06

Discipline & Academics

How performance is tracked, what accountability looks like day to day, and the three ways a Marine leaves the program.

The four measures

MeasureApplication
AdaptiveInternal measures track performance, attendance, and minor infractions. Evaluations are documented monthly or quarterly. Persistent issues are reviewed by leadership, potentially resulting in dismissal.
IntuitivePolicies proactively adjust to ensure fair opportunities for improvement. Standards remain constant; mission parameters and external factors are continually reassessed.
ResponsiveImmediate action for infractions that compromise mission readiness, viability, or security. Non-compliance is addressed without delay.
DecisiveRecommendations for removal or disciplinary action are made justly and acted upon swiftly.

Accountability & place of duty

TimeRequirement
0830Technical Accelerator members report to the senior Marine of their cohort. Also the accountability deadline for product teams on the day following a 72- or 96-hour liberty period.
0845The senior Marine of each product team reports daily accountability to the SEA. Accelerator cohort seniors consolidate anomalies and report cohort status by this time.
0930Staff Function Leads and Team Leads ensure 100% accountability to the MCSWF Operations Office.
If you are unaccounted for

Any Marine not accounted for is reported immediately to the SEA, who will attempt contact and continue until each Marine is positively accounted for. Team Leads document the infraction and forward it for your personnel file.

Place of duty is Innovation Tower in downtown Austin unless otherwise specified. Virtual or remote operations may be authorized case-by-case with leadership approval and should not be assumed as an entitlement.

Academic standards

  • Competency. Proficiency is demonstrated through homework, practical exercises, written exams, and performance evaluations. Attendance in all classes and training activities is mandatory.
  • Remediation. Score below 70 in any UT Technical Accelerator course and you undergo remedial training. A designated representative appointed by the SEA determines whether you are fit to graduate or proceed to the operational phase.
  • Evaluation. Marines are evaluated on the “Practice, People, Profession” methodology, distinguishing technical skills, interpersonal abilities, decision-making, and adherence to MCSWF values.

Leave & liberty

Student status

Leave will not be granted while a Marine is in student status — that is, while attending the Technical Accelerator and/or during the 1:1 SME pairing phase.

  • Standard leave. Taken during block leave periods such as winter holidays and 4th of July, and all federal holidays, with MCSWF staff approval.
  • Case-by-case leave. Requests during the Technical Accelerator or 1:1 SME pairing are processed individually.

All leave, liberty, and administrative absences are processed in accordance with MCO 6110.3A.

Course policies

  • Attendance. Regular attendance is crucial. Missing classes or labs may result in being dropped from the course.
  • Late assignments. A two-day grace period for lab assignments, with a 20% penalty.
  • Withdrawal. It is your responsibility to withdraw if necessary, and there may be financial or academic impacts.
  • Incompletes. Granted only for serious extenuating circumstances, and completed by a deadline set with the instructor.
  • Scholastic integrity. Plagiarism or any form of cheating results in a grade of F.

Instructional method

The course splits evenly between lectures and labs — half the class learning theory, half applying it. Coursework is supported via Blackboard, where you access slide decks, assignments, and grades.

ARTICLE 08

Advanced additional training

Product management and design are no longer a separate track. They are advanced training offered on top of the Software Engineer curriculum.

Every Marine here trains as a Software Engineer. Product management and design are the skills that make an engineer useful on a balanced team — knowing who the user is, what problem is worth solving, and how to shape a solution someone can actually use. This training covers PM basics, design basics, visual and UI design principles, collaborative leadership, and the tooling that goes with them.

Product management basics

  • Know the user before the solution. Discovery comes first — generative research to learn what people actually do, not what they say they would do.
  • Frame the problem, not the feature. Jobs to be Done describes what a user is hiring the product to accomplish.
  • Story mapping. Lay the user's journey out horizontally and slice releases vertically, so every release delivers a whole thin experience rather than half a feature.
  • Roadmaps are direction, not dates. A roadmap communicates intent and sequence. It is a planning instrument, not a commitment schedule.
  • Backlog management. An ordered, groomed backlog is the team's working agreement about what comes next and why.
  • Balanced team. Engineer, product manager, and designer share the decision. None of the three outranks the problem.

Design basics

  • Design research. Generative research to find the problem; evaluative research — usability testing — to find out whether your answer works.
  • Information architecture. How content is structured, labeled, and navigated. Most “confusing UI” is an IA problem.
  • Interaction design. Cognition, perception, and memory drive behavior. Design the interaction around how people actually process what is in front of them.
  • Visual design. Typography, color theory, hierarchy, and spacing — the universal principles that make an interface readable before it is decorative.
  • UI design. Navigation, forms, data display, and feedback patterns; micro-interactions and UX writing.
  • Responsive design. One product, every screen size. Layout adapts; the content and its priority do not change.
  • Design systems. Style guides and pattern libraries so the product stays coherent as more hands touch it.

Design principles

HierarchyEvery screen has one most important thing. Size, weight, color, and position tell the user what it is before they read a word.
ConsistencyThe same action looks and behaves the same way everywhere. Users learn a product once, not once per screen.
ContrastDifference carries meaning — between text and background, between a primary and a secondary action. Insufficient contrast is both a design failure and an accessibility failure.
Proximity & alignmentThings that belong together sit together. Alignment creates the invisible structure that makes a layout feel deliberate.
FeedbackEvery action gets a response. The user should never wonder whether the system heard them.
Constraint & affordanceMake the right action obvious and the wrong action difficult. The interface should suggest its own use.
SimplicityRemove until removing breaks it. Complexity that the user has to absorb is complexity you failed to absorb for them.

Modules to know

UX designStorytelling, ideation, user research and interaction design; information architecture, product strategy and best practice; creating user-centered experiences and presenting design decisions.
Design researchGenerative and evaluative research methods; user interviews, usability testing and analysis; presenting data and recommendations.
Visual & UI designVisual language for digital environments; universal principles, typography and color theory; style guides and pattern libraries; navigation, forms, data display and feedback patterns; micro-interactions, UX writing and conversational interfaces.
Interaction designThe role of psychology in design — cognition, perception and memory; designing and testing interactions that motivate user behavior.
Collaborative leadershipComparing the Military Decision Making Process (MDMP) with the Double Diamond UX framework; sketchnoting and visual facilitation; ethical standards in UX and PM.

Ethics & accessibility

You are building for Marines and for the public that Marines serve. A product that excludes part of that audience has failed, regardless of how well it performs.

  • Section 508. Federal law. Any electronic or information technology the government develops, procures, or uses must be accessible to people with disabilities. This is a requirement on your work, not a preference.
  • WCAG. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are the measurable standard behind 508 — perceivable, operable, understandable, robust. Design and test against them from the start; retrofitting accessibility costs far more than building it in.
  • Design ethics. No dark patterns. Do not design an interface that misleads a user into an action they did not intend, and do not collect more than the mission requires.
  • Inclusive by default. Sufficient color contrast, keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, and plain language are baseline, not enhancements.
  • Balanced team collaboration. Ethical standards in UX and PM are a shared responsibility. Anyone on the team can and should raise a concern about the work.

ARTICLE 10

Temporary duty (TAD)

Five steps, in order, with hard deadlines. Full detail lives in the TAD CONOPS SOP.

1 Create a Mock DTS Voucher
Before drafting a CONOPS, the requesting Marine creates a Mock DTS Voucher to capture a realistic cost estimate. This is the source data for the CONOPS template. DO NOT submit into DTS before Director approval.
2 Build and Submit the TAD CONOPS
Using the Mock DTS data and inputting the 5 Ws, the requesting Marine completes the MCSWF TAD CONOPS Template and submits it to the Director NLT 30 calendar days before the travel start date.
3 Director Review & Approval
The Director reviews the CONOPS and either approves or disapproves it, normally within 5 business days of receipt. A disapproved CONOPS is returned to the requester with the reason documented so it can be revised and resubmitted.
4 Log to the SharePoint TAD Tracker
Once approved, the requesting Marine logs the trip in the Sharepoint TAD Tracker within 2 business days, attaching or referencing the signed CONOPS.
5 Submit in DTS
With the CONOPS approved and the Tracker updated, the requesting Marine completes the official travel authorization in DTS.
Order matters

Do not submit into DTS before Director approval. The Mock DTS exists to produce the cost estimate for the CONOPS — it is not the authorization.
